extracted.intended_audience: Internet service providers (ISPs), telecommunications lawyers, regulatory compliance officers, FCC stakeholders, and policy makers
extracted.subtask_short: FCC Restoring Internet Freedom rule compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements from the FCC's 'Restoring Internet Freedom' Declaratory Ruling, Report and Order (WC Docket No. 17-108 / FCC 17-166), including the transparency rule, service definitions, classification tests, and associated procedural and compliance obligations. Intended to direct how broadband services are classified and what disclosures and practices providers must follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency disclosure requirement (§ 8.1(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person providing broadband internet access service shall publicly disclose accurate information regarding the network management practices, performance characteristics, and commercial terms of its broadband internet access services sufficient to enable consumers to make informed choices regarding the purchase and use of such services and entrepreneurs and other small businesses to develop, market, and maintain internet offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures must be made via a publicly available, easily accessible website or through transmittal to the Commission. The rule is intended to ensure consumers can make informed choices and that entrepreneurs and small businesses can develop offerings. The preamble further describes the content and means/format of disclosure (see discussion under 'Refining the Transparency Rule' and instructions on required disclosures, performance characteristics, network practices, and commercial terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'broadband internet access service' (§ 8.1(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadband internet access service is a mass-market retail service by wire or radio that provides the capability to transmit data to and receive data from all or substantially all internet endpoints, including any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service, but excluding dial-up internet access service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass-market means marketed and sold on a standardized basis to residential customers, small businesses, and other end-user customers (e.g., schools and libraries). The term includes services over any technology platform (wire, terrestrial wireless, satellite), covers fixed and mobile categories, and includes services purchased with E-rate or CAF support. Excludes enterprise/special access offerings, services that reach only one or a small number of endpoints (device-specific connectivity like e-readers or sensors), VPNs, CDNs, hosting/data storage, backbone services when separate from retail broadband, and certain non-retail premise operator arrangements. The Commission also notes that the transparency rule applies only to the limits of an ISP's control over transmission to/from its broadband customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable network management standard (§ 8.1(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A network management practice is reasonable if it is appropriate and tailored to achieving a legitimate network management purpose, taking into account the particular network architecture and technology of the broadband internet access service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test requires assessing whether a practice is appropriate and narrowly tailored to a legitimate technical objective given the specific network architecture/technology. This standard distinguishes reasonable technical management from practices that would improperly interfere with consumer use or competition; the preamble discusses evaluating purpose, tailoring, and network context when judging reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-service vs. telecommunications-service classification test
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying broadband internet access service, evaluate whether the service is an 'information service' under Section 3 of the Communications Act — i.e., whether it offers a capability for generating, acquiring, storing, transforming, processing, retrieving, utilizing, or making available information via telecommunications — versus a 'telecommunications service' which is the offering of telecommunications for a fee directly to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission adopts a broad reading of 'capability' (including potential ability and capacity designed for those purposes). Consider whether information-processing capabilities are provided or inextricably intertwined with transmission. Look to precedent (e.g., Brand X, MFJ) and concrete functionalities (DNS, caching, email, speed-test servers, parental controls, spam protection, etc.). Classification can consider whether those capabilities are part of the offering and whether customers rely on them; statutory interpretation should account for context and broader statutory purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: DNS and caching as integral/information-processing functionalities
rubrics_metrics.description: DNS is an indispensable functionality of broadband internet access service and, along with caching and other integrated features, constitutes information-processing capabilities that support an 'information service' classification rather than being merely telecommunications management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains DNS translates human-readable domain names to IP addresses and enables a majority of ordinary consumer internet uses; DNS provides address translation and other routing/distribution information. The Commission rejects treating DNS as solely a telecommunications management exception, analogizing it to MFJ 'address translation' gateway functions previously classified as information services. When evaluating classification, treat DNS/caching as customer-facing information-processing functionalities unless clearly internal to network operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from broadband internet access service (specialized services and non-mass-market services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Services that do not provide the capability to transmit to and receive data from all or substantially all internet endpoints are not broadband internet access service — examples include services offering connectivity to one or a small number of endpoints (device-specific connectivity), VPNs, CDNs, hosting/data storage services, internet backbone services when separate, and enterprise or special-access offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These services are generally not mass-market, are specific application-level services, or use network management to isolate capacity. The Commission continues prior precedent excluding such services from the broadband category, and the transparency rule only applies to the extent of an ISP's control over transmission for its broadband customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed vs. mobile broadband categorizations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For discussion and regulatory purpose, broadband internet access service is divided into 'fixed' and 'mobile' categories: 'fixed' serves end users primarily at fixed endpoints using stationary equipment; 'mobile' serves end users primarily using mobile stations (e.g., smartphones, mobile-network-enabled tablets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both categories cover any technology platform delivering those service types (cable, DSL, fiber, fixed wireless, unlicensed spectrum, satellite for fixed; mobile satellite and terrestrial mobile services for mobile). Public-safety services not commercially offered to the public are excluded. Classification findings apply to providers regardless of whether they lease or own facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required disclosure content: performance characteristics, network practices, and commercial terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadband providers must disclose performance characteristics, network practices, and commercial terms sufficient for consumer decision-making and for entrepreneurs/small businesses to develop, market, and maintain offerings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble and FRFA describe that the disclosure requirement replaces prior additional reporting obligations and the broadband label 'safe harbor.' Disclosures should be accurate and accessible; providers may post on their own websites or submit to the Commission (which will host them). The content/format expectations are discussed in the 'Refining the Transparency Rule' sections (content of required disclosures; means and format).

rubrics_metrics.name: No exemption for smaller providers from disclosure obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission declines to provide an exemption for smaller providers from the disclosure requirements adopted in the Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although classifying broadband as information service reduces some burdens, the disclosure requirement applies equally to all providers of broadband internet access service. The Order eliminates other burdensome Title II reporting obligations that previously applied, but retains the transparency rule without a small-provider exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of Title II conduct rules (general conduct, paid prioritization, blocking, throttling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order eliminates the general conduct standard and the specific conduct rules adopted in the Title II Order, including bans on paid prioritization, blocking, and throttling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale provided: (1) transparency combined with market competition and existing antitrust/consumer-protection laws provides comparable benefits at lower cost; (2) the record does not identify legal authority to adopt such conduct rules for all ISPs; (3) detailed cost–benefit analysis found the costs of each rule outweigh benefits. The Commission therefore declines to retain those conduct rules and instead relies on transparency and other legal frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of additional reporting obligations, direct notification requirement, and broadband label 'safe harbor'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order removes the additional reporting obligations, the direct notification requirement, and the broadband label 'safe harbor' that were part of the Title II Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal of these obligations reduces burdens on providers, particularly small entities. The transparency rule remains, but these specific reporting/formal notification mechanisms are no longer required. Providers still must make public disclosures as required in § 8.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of Open Internet Ombudsperson, formal complaint process, and advisory opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order eliminates the position of Open Internet Ombudsperson, the formal complaint process established under the Title II Order, and the issuance of advisory opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission concluded these mechanisms do not provide demonstrated benefits and that their functions can be handled by Commission staff. This change reduces formal procedural burdens on providers and the Commission alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement of mobile broadband classification as a private mobile service and restoration of 'interconnected service' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobile broadband internet access service is returned to its original classification as a private mobile radio service, and the definition of 'interconnected service' is restored to its prior formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reclassification removes various regulatory burdens applicable under Title II. Part 20 amendments revise definitions for 'Commercial mobile radio service,' 'Interconnected Service,' and 'Public Switched Network' to reflect restored classifications (e.g., interconnected service defined as that which gives subscribers capability to communicate to or receive communication from all other users on the public switched network).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Order's effective date is April 23, 2018, except for certain amendatory instructions (2, 3, 5, 6, and 8) that are delayed pending OMB approval of modified information collection requirements under the PRA (47 CFR 8.1 amendatory instruction 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some amendments become effective only upon the Commission publishing the announced effective date(s) after OMB approval. The Declaratory Ruling, Report and Order, and Order will also be effective upon the date announced in that same document for delayed items. Providers must monitor OMB/PRA developments for compliance timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible formats and accommodation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The full text is available for public inspection at the FCC Reference Information Center, and materials may be requested in accessible formats for people with disabilities (e.g., braille, large print, electronic files, audio) or reasonable accommodations (e.g., sign language interpreters, CART).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for accessible formats or accommodations are directed to fcc504@fcc.gov or to the Consumer & Governmental Affairs Bureau contact numbers provided. This ensures compliance with accessibility obligations and availability of the rule text in alternate formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timing for petitions and judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The period for filing petitions for reconsideration or petitions for judicial review of the Declaratory Ruling, Report and Order, and Order commences on the date that a summary of the Order is published in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the official start of the deadlines for seeking reconsideration or judicial review; parties should track Federal Register publication to determine filing windows.
